description: Designing fair questions, running a pilot, and cleaning a messy raw dataset before analysis begins.
content_html:
Designing a Good Questionnaire

A questionnaire is only as good as the questions it contains. Even with a perfect sample, a poorly designed questionnaire will produce data that is biased, incomplete, or simply not measuring what you intended. The specification identifies several key features to consider: leading questions, avoiding biased sources, the choice of open or closed questions, interview technique, and time factors.

Leading Questions

A leading question nudges the respondent towards a particular answer. Consider these two versions:

  • Leading: “Don’t you agree that students should do at least one hour of exercise a day?”
  • Neutral: “How many hours of exercise do you do on a typical day?”

The first version makes it socially awkward to disagree. Respondents who exercise very little may inflate their answers to avoid seeming lazy. The second makes no assumption. Always ask: does this question imply there is a right or preferred answer? If yes, rewrite it.

Which of these is leading? Think before reading on.

  • 1. “How often do you eat unhealthy food?” — Leading. The word “unhealthy” primes the respondent to under-report.
  • 2. “What type of food do you eat most often?” — Not leading. No assumption is built in.
  • 3. “Most young people spend too much time on their phones. How many hours do you spend on your phone per day?” — Leading. The preamble sets an expectation that shapes the answer.

Open and Closed Questions

Open questions invite free-text answers. The response might be detailed and revealing, but every answer is different — comparing many different written opinions requires careful judgement rather than straightforward statistical analysis.

Closed questions provide fixed options. The data is straightforward to count and compare. Always check that closed-question options are exhaustive (they cover all possible answers) and mutually exclusive (no answer fits more than one option).

Key Fact

Open questions: rich detail but hard to analyse statistically. Closed questions: easy to count and compare but may not capture every possible view. Good questionnaires often use both types.

Interview Technique and Time Factors

The way an interview is conducted can affect responses. Face-to-face interviews allow clarification of confusing questions, but the interviewer’s presence can cause socially desirable answers. Telephone or online questionnaires offer more anonymity, which may encourage more honest responses on sensitive topics, though response rates are often lower.

Time factors matter too. Asking about sleep habits on a Monday (after a weekend) will produce different answers from asking mid-week. Seasonal effects can skew data about outdoor activities, mental wellbeing, or energy consumption. A good questionnaire design considers when the questions will be asked and whether timing could bias the results.

Pilot Studies

A pilot study is a small-scale practice run — you administer the questionnaire to a small group before the main data collection. It serves several purposes:

  • Identifying ambiguous or unclear questions that respondents interpret differently.
  • Checking that response categories are exhaustive and mutually exclusive.
  • Estimating how long the questionnaire takes, so respondents can be informed.
  • Revealing leading or loaded language the researcher did not notice when writing the questions.

The pilot participants are typically not included in the main investigation. After the pilot, the questionnaire is revised before real data collection begins. Skipping the pilot is a common planning mistake — it is far cheaper to fix problems before 500 responses are collected than afterwards.

Cleaning Data

Raw data is rarely perfect. Before analysis begins, the dataset must be cleaned — checked and corrected for errors and inconsistencies. The specification identifies several types of problem that require data cleaning:

Missing data: Some respondents skip questions. A missing value cannot be included in calculations — you must decide whether to exclude the incomplete response, impute a value, or note the gap and acknowledge the effect on your results.

Non-responses: The entire questionnaire is not returned. If non-respondents share a characteristic, excluding them introduces bias.

Incorrect formats: A question asking for age might receive “sixteen” (text) alongside numerical entries. Spreadsheet software cannot calculate with inconsistent formats, so these must be standardised.

Extraneous notation: Currency symbols, spaces, or units entered inconsistently (“£4500” vs “4500” vs “4,500”) will prevent calculations. These must be removed or standardised before analysis.

Key Fact

Three main data cleaning problems: (1) missing data — blank cells where responses were skipped; (2) incorrect formats — inconsistent data entry; (3) extraneous notation — symbols or punctuation that prevent calculation.

Spotting Errors Using Row and Column Totals

One practical cleaning technique is to check whether values in a row or column are internally consistent. If the row total for a group is 45 but the three individual entries sum to 50, one entry is wrong. The specification notes that students may be asked to use row or column totals to identify a wrongly recorded value.

A worked example: a table records the number of books read by students in three year groups over two terms. If Year 9’s Term 1 column total is 120 but the individual class entries are 42, 38, and 45 (summing to 125), one of these three entries has been incorrectly recorded and needs investigating.

Control Groups and Extraneous Variables (Higher)

When an investigation compares two groups — for example, students who received a new study intervention versus those who did not — the group that does not receive the treatment is the control group. Without a control group, you cannot know whether any improvement is due to the intervention or would have happened anyway.

Extraneous variables — factors that could influence the outcome but are not the variable being tested — must be identified and held constant where possible. For example, if testing whether music helps concentration, room temperature and time of day are extraneous variables that should be kept the same across both groups.

An incomplete response is one where a participant returns the questionnaire but leaves some questions blank — perhaps because a question was unclear or felt too personal. A non-response is where the questionnaire is not returned at all.

Both create gaps in the data. Incomplete responses might be rescued for the questions that were answered, whereas non-responses produce no usable data. In both cases, if those affected share a characteristic, the results are biased.
exam_tip_html: On ‘Suggest and Justify’ questions about questionnaire design, a common error is giving a vague improvement such as “make the questions clearer”. You must identify the specific problem (e.g. “the question is leading because it implies one answer is preferred”) and the specific improvement (e.g. “rewrite as a neutral question with no implied preferred answer”). For data cleaning questions where a table is given, show your working: add up the row or column to demonstrate where the inconsistency lies.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Leading questions introduce bias by implying a preferred answer; closed questions produce data that is easier to analyse but must have exhaustive, mutually exclusive options; open questions produce richer but harder-to-analyse responses.
  • A pilot study is a small-scale trial run that identifies ambiguities, errors, and timing issues before the main data collection begins — skipping it risks finding problems when it is too late to fix them.
  • Raw data must be cleaned before analysis: missing values, incorrect formats, extraneous notation, and data entry errors identifiable by checking row and column totals must all be addressed before any statistical measures are calculated.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a leading question?
A) How many hours of sleep do you get on a typical school night?
B) Do you agree that teenagers need more sleep than adults?
C) At what time do you usually go to bed on weekdays?
D) How many times did you wake up during the night last week?
practice_questions.marks: B [1 mark] — Uses 'Do you agree that...' which implies a correct answer and primes respondents to agree.

practice_questions.text:
A student is cleaning a dataset and notices that in a table of test scores, the three entries for Group B are 24, 31, and 19, but the column total is listed as 78.
Work out whether the column total is correct, and if not, identify the discrepancy.
practice_questions.marks:
24 + 31 + 19 = 74 [1 mark].
The column total of 78 is incorrect; there is a discrepancy of 4 marks [1 mark].

practice_questions.text:
A researcher designs the following question for a survey: 'Most health experts recommend eating five portions of fruit and vegetables a day. How many portions did you eat yesterday?'
Describe one problem with this question and explain how it could be improved.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for identifying the problem and 2 marks for a developed explanation with an improvement.
Problem: the preamble about health experts is leading [1] because it sets a social norm (five portions) that respondents may feel they should meet, causing overstatement [1].
Improvement: remove the preamble and ask simply 'How many portions of fruit and vegetables did you eat yesterday?' so no expected answer is implied [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why a pilot study should be carried out before collecting the main data in an investigation.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 2 marks per reason, up to 4 marks.
Mastering: Two distinct reasons, each with a developed explanation.
- Ambiguous questions: the pilot reveals whether respondents interpret questions consistently [1]; if different people read the same question differently, the data will measure different things, undermining validity [1].
- Response categories: the pilot checks whether closed-question options are exhaustive [1]; if a common response is missing from the options, respondents force their answer into an ill-fitting category, producing inaccurate data [1].
- Timing: the pilot estimates completion time [1]; if the questionnaire takes much longer than expected, response rates in the main study will fall [1].
Secure: Two reasons, one developed. Developing: One reason with limited development. Emerging: States 'to check it works' without a developed reason.

practice_questions.text:
A class investigation asks 80 students to rate how often they exercise using the scale: Never / Rarely / Sometimes / Often / Always. After collection, 15 questionnaires have at least one blank response and 8 students did not return their questionnaire at all.
Suggest and justify two ways the investigator should handle these data issues before calculating any statistical measures.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per suggestion and 1 mark per justification linked to a specific data quality issue, up to 5 marks.
Mastering: Two strategies, each justified.
- For questionnaires with some blank responses: include them for the questions that were answered, excluding only specific missing values [1]; this preserves as much data as possible rather than wasting the partially complete response [1].
- For non-responses: note the 8 non-responders (out of 88) and consider whether they share a characteristic [1]; if less active students were less motivated to return the form, results will overestimate exercise frequency [1].
- Standardise coding: assign numerical codes consistently (1=Never to 5=Always) [1] so the same response is treated identically in every calculation [1].
Secure: Two strategies, one justified. Developing: One strategy with a justification. Emerging: Names missing data without suggesting how to handle it.

practice_questions.text:
A student is designing a questionnaire about students' diets. She includes the question: 'How many portions of fruit and vegetables do you eat? 0-2 / 3-4 / 5-7 / 7-10.'
Discuss at least two problems with this questionnaire design and suggest how each could be improved.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks for identified problems with developments and specific improvements.
Mastering: Two or more distinct problems identified and developed, each with a clear improvement and a judgement.
- Overlapping categories: '5-7' and '7-10' both include 7, so a respondent who eats exactly 7 portions does not know which to choose [1]; correct by making categories mutually exclusive: 0-2 / 3-4 / 5-7 / 8-10 [1].
- No 'more than' option: a student eating 11 or more portions cannot fit into any category [1]; add '10 or more' to make options exhaustive [1].
- Vague period: 'how many portions' does not specify a time frame [1]; add 'on a typical day' to standardise the reference period [1].
- Judgement: multiple design errors in one question will produce data that cannot be reliably analysed or compared across respondents [1].
Secure: Two problems, one developed improvement. Developing: One problem with an improvement. Emerging: Names the problem type without explaining what it means.

knowledge_checks.q: What is the main purpose of a pilot study?
options: To collect the main dataset before the full investigation begins
To select the sampling method that will be used
To trial the questionnaire on a small group and identify problems before the main data collection
To clean the data after it has been collected

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following best describes a leading question?
options: A question with more than four response options
A question that is worded to steer the respondent towards a particular answer
A question with no fixed response options
A question that is asked at the start of the survey

knowledge_checks.q: A closed question provides a fixed set of response options that must be _____ (covering all possible answers) and mutually exclusive.
Data that includes symbols, inconsistent units, or incorrectly formatted entries needs to be _____ before analysis.
Match each data quality issue to its correct description:
right: Blank cells where a participant skipped a question
Inconsistent data entry that software cannot process
An entire questionnaire not returned by the participant

flashcard_questions.a: A question worded to steer the respondent towards a particular answer, introducing bias.

flashcard_questions.q: What two features must closed-question response options have?
flashcard_questions.a: They must be exhaustive (cover all possibilities) and mutually exclusive (no overlap).
A small-scale trial of the questionnaire before the main data collection to identify and fix problems.

flashcard_questions.q: Name three types of problem that require data cleaning before analysis.
flashcard_questions.a: Missing data, incorrect formats, and extraneous notation such as currency symbols.

flashcard_questions.q: How can you identify a wrongly recorded value in a frequency table?
flashcard_questions.a: Check whether individual values sum to the stated row or column total; a discrepancy reveals an error.

flashcard_questions.q: What advantage does an open question have over a closed question?
flashcard_questions.a: It allows richer, more detailed responses in the respondent's own words.

flashcard_questions.q: What disadvantage does an open question have compared to a closed question?
flashcard_questions.a: Answers are harder to analyse statistically because every response may differ.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is face-to-face interviewing sometimes less appropriate for sensitive topics?
flashcard_questions.a: Respondents may give socially desirable answers rather than honest ones when watched.
The group in an experiment that does not receive the treatment, used as a baseline for comparison.
Variables that could affect the response variable but are not the investigation's focus; they must be controlled.

glossary_terms.definition: A question that is worded in a way that steers the respondent towards a particular answer, introducing bias into the data.
Questions that allow the respondent to answer in their own words, producing qualitative data that is rich but harder to analyse statistically.
Questions that provide a fixed set of response options for the respondent to choose from, producing data that is easier to analyse statistically.
A small-scale trial run of a questionnaire or data collection method, conducted before the main investigation to identify and fix problems.
A group in an experiment that does not receive the treatment being tested, used as a baseline to measure the effect of the treatment.
Variables that influence the response variable but are not the focus of the investigation and must be identified and controlled.
